onions.title: Why Do Onions Make You Cry? It's a Gas! 🧅 #shorts
sentences: You're not crying because onions are sad.
You're crying because of a tiny chemical defense.
An onion keeps sulfur compounds and an enzyme locked in separate parts of its cells.
When your knife breaks those cells, they mix.
The enzymes turn the sulfur into a gas called propanethial S-oxide.
It floats straight up toward your face.
On your eyes, it dissolves in the thin layer of water and forms a mild acid.
Your eyes fight back the only way they can: tears.
The trick? Chill the onion first.
Cold slows the enzymes, so less gas.
And garlic? Its sulfur compound doesn't make this gas at all.
Got a kitchen why? Ask in the comments.
onions.description:
It's not the juice. Cutting an onion mixes sulfur compounds with enzymes, creating a gas that turns into a mild acid on your eyes. Here's the chemistry, plus the one trick that actually helps.

brainfreeze.title: Why Does Ice Cream Give You Brain Freeze? 🍦 #shorts
sentences: Brain freeze has a real medical name.
Sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia.
Try saying that with a mouth full of ice cream.
When something very cold hits the roof of your mouth, it chills the nerves and blood vessels back there.
The vessels squeeze tight, then quickly widen again.
Your nerves send that signal to the brain, but the brain feels it as pain in your forehead.
In one study, kids who ate ice cream in under five seconds got brain freeze more than twice as often as slow eaters.
Quick fix: press your tongue against the roof of your mouth, or sip something warm.
Now you know. Eat slow.
brainfreeze.description:
Brain freeze is real, and it has a very long name. Cold on the roof of your mouth chills nerves and blood vessels, and your brain reads it as forehead pain. Here's why, and how to stop it fast.

ocean.title: If Rivers Are Fresh, Why Is the Ocean Salty? 🌊 #shorts
sentences: Rivers are fresh water.
And they all flow into the ocean.
So why is the ocean salty?
Blame the rain.
Rain is very slightly acidic, so over a very long time it slowly eats away at rocks on land.
That releases tiny bits of minerals, called ions.
Rivers carry them all the way to the sea.
When seawater evaporates, the water leaves, but the salt stays behind.
More minerals also leak in from cracks in the sea floor, where magma heats the water.
Today, about three and a half percent of seawater's weight is salt.
Mostly sodium and chloride. The same stuff you sprinkle on your fries.
ocean.description:

windowhole.title: What's the Tiny Hole in Airplane Windows? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Next time you fly, look closely at the window.
There's a tiny hole near the bottom.
Don't worry. It's supposed to be there.
A plane window is actually three layers.
The outer pane is the strong one. It holds back the pressure.
The middle pane is a backup, in case the outer one fails.
The tiny hole is in that middle pane. It's called a breather hole.
It lets air through, so the pressure on both sides of the middle pane stays equal.
That way, all the force lands on the outer pane, and the backup stays ready for an emergency.
At cruising height, the air outside has only about a third of the pressure inside the cabin.
That's a lot of push on one small window. Part two of our airplane window series.
windowhole.description:
That tiny hole in your airplane window has a job. Plane windows have three panes, and the breather hole keeps the backup pane ready for an emergency.

fingers.title: Why Do Your Fingers Wrinkle in Water? 🖐️ #shorts
sentences: Wrinkly fingers in the bath aren't just soggy skin.
Your nervous system is doing it on purpose.
After about five minutes in water, your nerves tell the blood vessels in your fingertips to squeeze tight.
The fingertip shrinks a little, and the skin on top folds into wrinkles.
How do we know nerves control it?
People with damaged nerves in their hands don't get wrinkly fingers at all.
But why would your body do this?
One idea: the wrinkles work like tire treads, draining water away for a better grip on wet things.
In one test, people with wrinkly fingers moved wet marbles faster.
But another study found no difference. So scientists are still arguing.
What do you think? Tell us in the comments.
fingers.description:

bridge.title: Why Don't Bridges Twist in the Wind Anymore? 🌉 #shorts
sentences: In 1940, a brand-new bridge started dancing in the wind.
Locals called it Galloping Gertie.
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington state was long, light, and very thin.
On November seventh, a wind of about forty miles an hour hit it.
Not a hurricane. Just a strong wind.
First, the road waved up and down. Then it started to twist.
One side rose as the other dropped, tilting up to forty-five degrees.
Wind swirling off the bridge's solid sides pushed in rhythm with the twist, making it bigger and bigger.
Just after eleven a.m., a six-hundred-foot piece of the road fell into the water.
The people on the bridge escaped, and engineers learned a hard lesson.
Today, big bridge designs are tested as models in wind tunnels, and built stiff against twisting.
That's why bridges don't dance anymore.

pisa.title: Why Hasn't the Leaning Tower of Pisa Fallen? 🏛️ #shorts
sentences: The Leaning Tower of Pisa has been tilting for over eight hundred years.
So why hasn't it fallen down?
Building started in 1173.
Just five years later, after the third floor, the ground under one side started to sink.
The tower sits on soft clay and sand, and the south side gave way.
Then a war stopped construction for almost a hundred years.
That pause probably saved it. The soil had time to settle and firm up.
By 1990, it was leaning five and a half degrees, and it was closed to visitors.
So engineers did something clever. They carefully pulled soil out from under the high side.
The tower slowly settled back, about nineteen inches straighter.
It reopened in 2001, and engineers expect it to stay stable for about two hundred years.
pisa.description:
It's been tilting since the 1170s, so why hasn't the Leaning Tower of Pisa fallen? Soft soil, a century-long war break, and a clever engineering fix.

molasses.title: Why Was a Wave of Molasses So Deadly? 🍯 #shorts
sentences: In 1919, a wave of molasses swept through a Boston neighborhood.
It sounds like a joke. It wasn't.
On January fifteenth, a giant tank holding about two point three million gallons of molasses burst open.
A sticky wave, reported at up to forty feet tall, rushed through the streets at around thirty-five miles an hour.
Twenty-one people died, and about a hundred and fifty were injured.
But why was syrup so deadly?
The molasses was warmer than the freezing winter air.
As it spread out, it cooled fast, and became four or more times thicker.
People caught in it could barely move, and rescuers struggled to reach them.
An engineer later found the tank's steel walls were dangerously thin, about half as thick as they should have been.
In 2016, Harvard researchers recreated the flood with corn syrup in a cold room, and confirmed it.
That's how cold weather turned syrup into a trap.
molasses.description:

titanic.title: Why Did the Titanic Sink So Fast? 🚢 #shorts
sentences: The Titanic sank in just two hours and forty minutes. Why so fast?
Late on April fourteenth, 1912, it hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic.
Its hull was split into sixteen compartments, and it could stay afloat with four of them flooded.
The iceberg opened up at least five.
As the bow sank lower, water spilled over the top of each wall into the next, like an ice cube tray.
And there were only twenty lifeboats, room for barely half the people on board.
More than fifteen hundred people died.
Two years later, a new treaty required lifeboats for everyone, and radio watch around the clock.
All because...

manhole.title: Why Are Manhole Covers Round? 🕳️ #shorts
sentences: Every manhole cover is round for one life-saving reason.
A single cover can weigh two to three hundred pounds.
Now picture a square one.
Its diagonal is longer than its sides. Turn it just right, and it slips straight down the hole.
Onto whoever is working below.
A circle is the same width in every direction, so it can never fall through its hole.
Bonus: you can roll it, and it fits back in at any angle.
And that's exactly why...
manhole.description:

jetblast.title: Why Is Jet Blast So Dangerous? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: This week, the blast from a jet's engines knocked over a small plane on the ground. How?
A jet engine moves forward by throwing air backward, very fast.
Even at just forty percent power, a big jet can push air at up to a hundred and twenty miles an hour.
And that wind reaches two hundred feet behind it.
That's hurricane-force wind.
A NASA safety study found most jet blast damage hits other aircraft, especially light ones under five thousand pounds.
That's why pilots keep their distance, and never park tail-first behind a jet.
Which is exactly how...

whiteplanes.title: Why Are Most Planes Painted White? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Almost every airliner in the world is painted white. Why?
First, heat. White reflects sunlight, so the cabin stays cooler on the ground.
Second, safety. Cracks, dents and oil leaks are easy to spot on white.
Third, weight. The paint on a big jet can weigh up to twelve hundred pounds.
That's like carrying eight extra passengers on every flight.
So airlines keep the paint simple, because every extra layer burns more fuel.
And dark colors fade faster in the sun, so they need repainting sooner.
And that's why...
whiteplanes.description:

cabinlights.title: Why Do Planes Dim the Lights Before Landing? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Right before landing at night, the cabin lights go dim. Why?
It's not to help you sleep. It's a safety rule.
Nearly half of fatal airliner accidents happen during final approach and landing.
If something goes wrong, you may have to escape in darkness or smoke.
So the crew gets your eyes used to the dark before anything happens.
Dim light also makes the glowing exit signs and floor lights easier to see.
And the window shades stay open, so the crew can spot fire outside before opening a door.
And that's why...
cabinlights.description:
Cabin lights are dimmed for night takeoffs and landings so your eyes are already used to the dark if you have to evacuate, and so the lit exit signs and floor path stand out. Boeing data for 2004-2013 shows 47% of fatal airliner accidents happened during final approach and landing.

fl350.title: Why Do Planes Fly at 35,000 Feet? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Planes cruise at thirty-five thousand feet, higher than Mount Everest. Why?
Up there, the air is much thinner, so there's less drag.
Less drag means the plane flies faster and burns less fuel.
It's also above most of the weather, so the ride is smoother.
But planes can't just keep climbing.
Go too high, and the air is too thin for the wings to lift and the engines to push.
So pilots pick the sweet spot, and climb a little higher as the fuel burns off.
And that's why...
fl350.description:
At cruising altitude the air is thin, so there is less drag and the plane burns less fuel, and it sits above most weather. But too high and the wings and engines run out of air, so pilots fly at a sweet spot and step up as the plane gets lighter.

earspop.title: Why Do Your Ears Pop on a Plane? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Your ears pop on almost every flight. Why?
Behind your eardrum is a small pocket of air.
When the plane climbs or descends, the cabin pressure changes faster than that pocket can keep up.
The difference pushes on your eardrum. That's the pressure and pain you feel.
The fix is a tiny tube from your ear to the back of your nose.
When you swallow or yawn, it opens, the pressure evens out, and pop.
Children have shorter, flatter tubes, which is one reason babies often cry during landing.
And that's why...
earspop.description:
When a plane climbs or descends, cabin pressure changes faster than the air behind your eardrum can adjust. Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tube and evens it out. General information only, not medical advice.

smoking.title: Why Is Smoking Banned on Planes? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Why is smoking banned on planes? It started with one fire.
In July nineteen seventy-three, a Boeing seven oh seven was minutes from landing in Paris.
A fire started in a rear toilet, most likely from a cigarette thrown in the waste bin.
Smoke filled the cabin before the pilots could land.
One hundred and twenty-three people died. Only eleven survived.
That same year, America banned smoking in airplane toilets.
By two thousand, it was banned on every American airline flight. But ashtrays are still required, in case someone breaks the rule.
And that's...

tenerife.title: Why Do Pilots Repeat Every Instruction? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Pilots repeat almost everything the tower tells them. Why?
In nineteen seventy-seven, two jumbo jets were on the same foggy runway in Tenerife.
Nobody could see anybody. Not the pilots, not the tower.
One crew began its takeoff without clearance. The other jet's radio warning was blocked by another call at the same moment.
Five hundred and eighty-three people died. It is still the deadliest accident in aviation history.
After that, radio rules changed around the world.
The word takeoff is now used only when a plane is truly cleared to go, and pilots read key instructions back.
And that's why...
tenerife.description:
On 27 March 1977, two Boeing 747s collided on a fog-covered runway at Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife. 583 people died and 61 survived. A blocked radio call and unclear wording were part of the chain, so phraseology was standardized worldwide: 'takeoff' is said only with a real clearance, and key instructions are read back.

food.title: Why Does Airplane Food Taste So Bland? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Airplane food tastes bland, and it's not the chef's fault. Why?
At cruise, the cabin is pressurized like a mountain eight thousand feet high.
The air is also cool and very dry, which dulls your nose and your taste buds.
German researchers found that salty and sweet tastes drop by about thirty percent.
Even the engine noise changes flavor.
In a Cornell study, loud jet noise made sweet things taste weaker, but savory umami taste stronger.
That's why tomato juice is so popular in the air. One airline serves about as much of it as beer.
And that's why...
food.description:

row13.title: Why Is There No Row 13 on Many Planes? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: On many planes, row twelve is followed by row fourteen. Why?
It's not a mistake. Airlines skip the number on purpose.
In much of the Western world, thirteen is seen as unlucky.
One big airline said it plainly: rows thirteen and seventeen are missing because they are considered unlucky numbers.
Seventeen? That one comes from Italy.
In Roman numerals, seventeen can be rearranged to spell a Latin word that means, my life is over.
The seats are exactly the same. Only the number changes.
And that's why...
row13.description:
Many airlines skip row 13, and some skip 17 too, because the numbers are considered unlucky. Lufthansa confirmed it in 2017. The 17 comes from Italy: XVII can be rearranged into VIXI, Latin for 'my life is over'.

contrails.title: Why Do Planes Leave White Trails? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Some planes draw long white lines across the sky. Why?
It's not smoke. It's mostly ice.
Jet exhaust contains a lot of water vapor.
At cruising height, the air is colder than minus thirty-five degrees, so the vapor freezes into tiny ice crystals.
And the trail can even tell you about the weather up there.
If the high air is dry, the trail vanishes quickly.
If it is humid, the trail can stay for hours and spread into thin clouds.
And that's why...
contrails.description:
Contrails are ice: water vapor in jet exhaust freezes in air colder than about -34°F (-36.5°C) at cruising altitude. In dry air they vanish quickly; in humid air they can last for hours and spread into thin cloud.

boardleft.title: Why Do You Always Board a Plane from the Left? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: You almost always board a plane through the left door. Why?
The habit comes from ships. For centuries, people boarded on the left, the port side.
Planes kept the tradition.
It also helps the captain, who sits in the left seat and can line the door up with the jet bridge.
And it keeps you away from the busy side.
Fuel trucks and baggage loaders work on the right side of the plane.
So passengers stay on the left, and the ground crew can work without anyone in the way.
And that's why...
boardleft.description:
Boarding on the left comes from ships, which were boarded on the port side. It also lets the captain, in the left seat, line the door up with the jet bridge, and it keeps passengers away from fueling and baggage loading on the right.

wingsbend.title: Why Do Airplane Wings Bend So Much? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Look out the window in turbulence, and the wing is bending. Should you worry?
No. Wings are built to bend.
A wing that flexes takes the load and springs back, instead of fighting every bump with heavy metal.
The rules say a wing must survive one and a half times the worst load it should ever meet.
So engineers pull the wings up until they prove it.
In twenty ten, Boeing bent the wings of a seven eight seven upward by about twenty-five feet.
The wing passed. A stiffer wing would only be heavier, and burn more fuel.
So next time...
wingsbend.description:
Wings are designed to flex and spring back. Certification requires a wing to carry 150% of the highest load expected in service; in March 2010 Boeing flexed the 787's wings upward by about 25 feet (7.6 m) in that test.

gimli.title: Why Did a Jet Run Out of Fuel in Mid-Air? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: In nineteen eighty-three, a passenger jet ran out of fuel at forty-one thousand feet. How?
The fuel gauges were not working, so the fuel was measured by hand.
But the math mixed up pounds and kilograms.
The plane took off with less than half the fuel it needed.
Halfway there, both engines went silent.
The captain also flew gliders. He glided the big jet for seventeen minutes to an old air base at Gimli.
Part of it had become a race track. The jet landed anyway, and all sixty-nine people on board survived.
And that's how...
gimli.description:
On 23 July 1983, Air Canada Flight 143, a Boeing 767, ran out of fuel at 41,000 feet after a pounds/kilograms mix-up left it with about 45% of the fuel it needed. The crew glided 17 minutes to a former air base at Gimli, Manitoba. All 69 on board survived. It is known as the Gimli Glider.

aloharoof.title: Why Did a Plane's Roof Tear Off in Flight? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: In nineteen eighty-eight, a jet landed with part of its roof missing. How did that happen?
The plane was nineteen years old, and flew short island hops in Hawaii.
It had made almost ninety thousand flights in warm, salty air.
Every flight strains the metal skin a little, and salt air adds corrosion.
At twenty-four thousand feet, eighteen feet of roof tore away.
One flight attendant was lost. Seat belts held the passengers in, and the pilots landed thirteen minutes later.
After that, older planes got special inspections, to find tiny cracks before they grow.
And that's how...
aloharoof.description:

One flight attendant died; the other 94 people on board survived. The accident led to special inspection rules for aging aircraft.

winglets.title: Why Do Wing Tips Curve Up? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Look at the tip of a modern airliner's wing. It bends upward. Why?
Under a wing, the air pressure is high. On top, it is low.
At the tip, the high-pressure air spills around the edge and forms a spinning vortex.
That swirl drags on the plane, and wastes fuel.
In the nineteen seventies, a NASA engineer named Richard Whitcomb found a fix.
He added a small upturned fin, the winglet. In flight tests, it cut drag by about six to seven percent.
Today, a winglet upgrade cuts fuel burn by about four to six percent on a typical airliner.
And that's why...
winglets.description:
Air spilling around a wingtip forms a vortex that adds drag. NASA's Richard Whitcomb developed the winglet in the 1970s; flight tests in 1979-80 showed about 6-7% less cruise drag, and a typical retrofit cuts fuel burn by about 4-6%.

shades.title: Why Must Window Shades Be Open for Landing? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Before takeoff and landing, the crew asks you to open your window shade. Why?
It's not about the view. It's a safety check.
Takeoff and landing are the riskiest minutes of a flight.
If the plane has to be evacuated, the crew must decide which exits are safe to use.
And they decide by looking outside.
A fire on one side means the exits on that side stay shut.
Open shades also let you see which side is safe, before you move.
And that's why...
shades.description:
Window shades are raised for takeoff and landing so the crew can look outside and assess where any danger is, such as a fire, before choosing which exits to open, and so passengers can see which side is safe.

phonemode.title: Why Do Phones Need Airplane Mode? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: On every flight, you're told to switch your phone to airplane mode. Does it really matter?
The rule is older than mobile phones. It began in nineteen sixty-one, to ban F M radios on board.
Those radios used frequencies close to the ones pilots use.
Phones use very different frequencies, so experts call real interference extremely unlikely.
Two American studies, in two thousand six and twenty twelve, found no evidence that phones disturb aircraft systems.
Some pilots say phones can cause a buzz in their headsets, like a mosquito. Others doubt it.
In America the rule is still in force. Europe lifted its ban in twenty twenty-two.
And yet...
phonemode.description:
The rule behind airplane mode dates from May 1961, when the FAA banned FM radio receivers on board. FAA-commissioned studies in 2006 and 2012 found no evidence that phone signals interfere with aircraft systems; some pilots report headset buzz. The EU lifted its ban in 2022.

ashtray.title: Why Are There Still Ashtrays on Planes? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: Smoking on planes is banned. So why does every plane still have an ashtray?
Look at the toilet door on your next flight. It's there.
The rules require it, even on brand new planes.
The reason goes back to a fire in nineteen seventy-three. A cigarette in a toilet waste bin is believed to have started it.
One hundred and twenty-three people died.
So the rule makers assume that one day, someone will break the ban.
And when they do, the cigarette must go into a metal ashtray, not into a bin full of paper.
And that's why...

oxygen.title: Why Do Oxygen Masks Last Only Minutes? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: The oxygen masks on a plane only work for about fifteen minutes. Is that enough?
There is no oxygen tank above your seat. There is a small chemical generator.
When you pull the mask down, a pin fires, and chemicals start making oxygen.
It gets very hot, over four hundred degrees, so a burning smell is normal.
And once it starts, it cannot be switched off.
It runs for about twelve to twenty minutes. That is enough, because the pilots dive to about ten thousand feet, where you can breathe normally.
That descent takes around ten minutes. And oxygen flows even if the bag does not inflate.
And that's why...
oxygen.description:

sentences: In nineteen ninety, a captain was pulled halfway out of his own cockpit window, and survived. How?
The jet was climbing through seventeen thousand feet over England.
Suddenly, the left windscreen blew out.
The captain was dragged out, with only his legs still inside. A flight attendant grabbed him and held on.
The crew held him for about twenty minutes, while the co-pilot landed the plane.
Everyone survived, and the captain was flying again within five months.
The cause? The windscreen had been fitted the day before, and eighty-four of its ninety screws were slightly too small.
And that's how...

All 87 on board survived. 84 of the 90 windscreen screws were 0.026 inch too small in diameter.

ba009.title: Why Did All Four Engines Stop at Once? ✈️ #shorts
sentences: In nineteen eighty-two, all four engines of a jumbo jet stopped at thirty-seven thousand feet. Why?
It was night over Indonesia. The weather radar showed clear skies.
Then a strange glow appeared on the windscreen, and smoke filled the cabin.
One by one, all four engines failed.
The plane had flown into a cloud of volcanic ash.
Dry ash is invisible to weather radar. It melted inside the engines and choked them.
The jet glided down for more than ten minutes. Then the ash broke off, the engines restarted, and all two hundred and sixty-three people landed safely.
And that's why pilots fear ash, ever since...
ba009.description:
On 24 June 1982, British Airways Flight 009, a Boeing 747, lost all four engines at 37,000 feet after flying into volcanic ash from Mount Galunggung, Indonesia. Dry ash does not show on weather radar. The engines restarted after a long glide and all 263 people on board landed safely in Jakarta.
